note: Founded in 2017. Every Steeler in the Pro Football Hall of Fame is automatically included. Players must be retired three seasons and have played at least three seasons in Pittsburgh.

members.name: Jerome Bettis
members.text: Came over from the Rams in a 1996 draft-day trade and ran for 10,571 yards in Pittsburgh. “The Bus” was nearly impossible to tackle near the goal line. He ended his career with a Super Bowl XL win in his hometown of Detroit.

members.name: Rocky Bleier
members.text: A 1968 draft pick who was badly wounded in Vietnam and was told he might never play again. He worked his way back into the starting backfield, ran for 1,036 yards in 1976 and caught a touchdown pass in Super Bowl XIII. He won four rings.

members.name: Mel Blount
members.text: A big, physical cornerback who was the 1975 Defensive Player of the Year. He was so tough on receivers that the league changed its contact rules in 1978. His 57 interceptions are still the team record, and he won four Super Bowls.

members.name: Terry Bradshaw
members.text: The first overall pick in 1970 grew into the quarterback of a dynasty. He won four Super Bowls, was MVP of XIII and XIV, and was the league MVP in 1978. His deep passing made the late-’70s offense one of the NFL’s most dangerous.

members.name: Larry Brown
members.text: Started as a blocking tight end and caught a touchdown pass in Super Bowl IX. The team later moved him to right tackle, where he made the Pro Bowl. He is one of the few players to start at two positions on title teams, and he won four rings.

members.name: Jack Butler
members.text: An undrafted cornerback from St. Bonaventure who became one of the best ball hawks of the 1950s. He picked off 52 passes before a knee injury ended his career. He was inducted into Canton in 2012.

members.name: Kevin Colbert
members.pos: Director of football operations, general manager
members.text: Ran the football department for 22 seasons, first as director of football operations and then as general manager. His drafts and signings built the rosters that won Super Bowls XL and XLIII and reached XLV. The team made the playoffs in most of his seasons in charge.

members.name: Myron Cope
members.text: The voice of Steelers radio for 35 seasons, famous for “Yoi!” and “Double yoi!” He came up with the Terrible Towel in 1975. He gave the rights to the Towel to a school that serves people with disabilities, and it still benefits from sales today.

members.name: Bill Cowher
members.text: A Pittsburgh-area native who took over for Chuck Noll in 1992 at age 34. His jaw-out intensity defined the team for 15 seasons, which included 10 playoff trips and two Super Bowl appearances. He won Super Bowl XL and made the Pro Football Hall of Fame in 2020.

members.name: Sam Davis
members.text: An undrafted guard from Allen University who became the starting left guard and a team captain. He blocked for the first three Super Bowl winners. He was a steady presence on the line for 13 seasons.

members.name: Dermontti Dawson
members.text: Followed Mike Webster at center and somehow kept the standard just as high. He was fast enough to pull and lead the way on running plays, which was rare for a center. He made seven straight Pro Bowls and went into Canton in 2012.

members.name: Buddy Dial
members.text: A big-play receiver of the late 1950s and early 1960s who averaged more than 20 yards per catch as a Steeler. He topped 1,000 receiving yards twice. He was one of the top deep threats of his era.

members.name: Bill Dudley
members.text: “Bullet Bill” did everything: run, pass, catch, return kicks and intercept passes. He led the league in rushing as a rookie in 1942. After returning from military service, he was named the league’s MVP in 1946.

members.name: Alan Faneca
members.text: A 1998 first-round pick who became one of the best guards in football. His pulling block helped spring Willie Parker’s 75-yard touchdown run in Super Bowl XL. He made seven Pro Bowls as a Steeler and was inducted into Canton in 2021.

members.name: James Farrior
members.text: Signed from the Jets in 2002 and became the voice of the defense, calling the signals for a decade. He was runner-up for Defensive Player of the Year in 2004. The longtime captain won two Super Bowls.

members.name: Jason Gildon
members.text: A pass-rushing outside linebacker who made three Pro Bowls. When he left Pittsburgh, he was the franchise’s career sack leader. He linked the Blitzburgh defenses of the 1990s with the defenses of the 2000s.

members.name: Joe Greene
members.text: Chuck Noll’s first draft pick, in 1969, and the cornerstone of the Steel Curtain. “Mean Joe” was Defensive Player of the Year twice and set the tone for four Super Bowl champions. He later coached the defensive line for Noll.

members.name: Kevin Greene
members.text: Spent just three seasons in Pittsburgh but made them count. The free-agent pass rusher led the NFL with 14 sacks in 1994 and helped the team reach Super Bowl XXX. His career sack total took him to Canton in 2016.

members.name: L.C. Greenwood
members.text: A 10th-round pick who became a six-time Pro Bowl defensive end, known for his gold high-top cleats. He was the Steel Curtain’s top pass rusher and was a force in the Super Bowls. He won four rings.

members.name: Jack Ham
members.text: An outside linebacker so smart and smooth that he almost never seemed out of position. He finished with 32 interceptions and 21 fumble recoveries and was the 1975 Defensive Player of the Year. He won four Super Bowls.

members.name: Casey Hampton
members.text: A 2001 first-round pick who anchored the 3-4 defense at nose tackle for 12 seasons. He took on double teams so the linebackers could make plays. He made five Pro Bowls and won two Super Bowls.

members.name: Franco Harris
members.text: Made the Immaculate Reception as a rookie in 1972, the play that changed the franchise. He was MVP of Super Bowl IX and ran for 11,950 yards in Pittsburgh, still the team record. His No. 32 was retired in 2022.

members.name: James Harrison
members.text: An undrafted player who was cut several times before he stuck. He became the 2008 Defensive Player of the Year and returned an interception 100 yards for a touchdown in Super Bowl XLIII. He is the franchise’s career sack leader.

members.name: Dick Hoak
members.text: A tough, versatile running back in the 1960s who later coached the team’s running backs for 35 years. Across both roles, he spent more than four decades with the team. He coached backs on five Super Bowl winners.

members.name: Tunch Ilkin
members.text: Born in Istanbul, he was a sixth-round pick who became a two-time Pro Bowl right tackle. He then spent decades as a beloved radio analyst. He was known around Pittsburgh for his faith and his charity work.

members.name: John Henry Johnson
members.text: A bruising fullback who gave Pittsburgh its first 1,000-yard rushing seasons, in 1962 and 1964. He was also a punishing blocker. He went into Canton in 1987.

members.name: Walt Kiesling
members.text: A Hall of Fame lineman who finished his playing career in Pittsburgh. He served as head coach in three different stints. He was involved with the team for most of its first three decades.

members.name: Jon Kolb
members.text: A third-round pick from Oklahoma State who started at left tackle on four Super Bowl champions. He was one of the strongest men in the league. He later coached for the team.

members.name: Carnell Lake
members.text: A hard-hitting safety who made five Pro Bowls. In 1995, he moved to cornerback to fill a hole in the lineup, and the team reached Super Bowl XXX. He later returned as the team’s defensive backs coach.

members.name: Jack Lambert
members.text: The snarling, gap-toothed middle linebacker of the Steel Curtain. He was the 1976 Defensive Player of the Year and made nine straight Pro Bowls. He won four Super Bowls.

members.name: Bobby Layne
members.text: A Hall of Fame quarterback who came over from Detroit in a 1958 trade. He gave Pittsburgh a fiery veteran leader and also handled the kicking. He played his final five seasons as a Steeler.

members.name: Dick LeBeau
members.text: The father of the modern zone blitz, a pressure scheme that fooled offenses for two decades. As defensive coordinator, he ran the defenses that won Super Bowls XL and XLIII. He is in Canton for his playing career as a Lions cornerback.

members.name: Louis Lipps
members.text: The 1984 NFL Offensive Rookie of the Year. He was a big-play receiver and a dangerous punt returner. He made two Pro Bowls in the 1980s.

members.name: Greg Lloyd
members.text: A sixth-round pick from Fort Valley State who became the fierce heart of the Blitzburgh defenses. He made five Pro Bowls. He helped lead the team to Super Bowl XXX.

members.name: Ray Mansfield
members.text: “The Old Ranger” held down center through the 1960s and into the first two Super Bowl wins. He played in more than 180 straight games. He also helped train his successor, Mike Webster.

members.name: Ray Mathews
members.text: A versatile offensive weapon of the 1950s who lined up at halfback and at end. He was one of the team’s top playmakers through the decade. He made the Pro Bowl as a Steeler.

members.name: Johnny “Blood” McNally
members.text: A colorful Hall of Fame halfback from the league’s early days. He played for the Pirates and served as their player-coach from 1937 to 1939. He is better known for his years with the Packers.

members.name: Heath Miller
members.text: A 2005 first-round pick who became a dependable target and a strong blocker for 11 seasons. Fans greeted his catches with long chants of “Heeeath.” He holds the team record for catches by a tight end and won two Super Bowls.

members.name: Gerry Mullins
members.text: A fourth-round pick from USC who played guard, tackle and tight end. That flexibility made him valuable on the line. He won four Super Bowls.

members.name: Elbie Nickel
members.text: A sure-handed tight end from the late 1940s and 1950s who was one of the team’s top receivers of his era. He spent his whole 11-season career in Pittsburgh. He made multiple Pro Bowls.

members.name: Chuck Noll
members.text: Took over a losing franchise in 1969 and built a dynasty through the draft. He won four Super Bowls in six seasons, still the most in league history at the time. He coached 23 seasons and was inducted into Canton in 1993.

members.name: Bill Nunn
members.text: A Pittsburgh Courier sportswriter who joined the scouting staff and opened doors at historically Black colleges. He helped find players like John Stallworth, Donnie Shell and L.C. Greenwood. He was inducted into Canton in 2021.

members.name: Willie Parker
members.text: An undrafted back from North Carolina who became a three-time 1,000-yard rusher. His 75-yard touchdown run in Super Bowl XL was the longest run in Super Bowl history at the time. He won two rings.

members.name: Troy Polamalu
members.text: A 2003 first-round pick whose long hair and wild instincts made him one of the most famous defenders of his era. He was the 2010 Defensive Player of the Year and made eight Pro Bowls. He won two Super Bowls and was inducted into Canton in 2020.

members.name: Joey Porter Sr.
members.text: A loud, physical outside linebacker who led the defense’s pass rush for eight seasons. He made three Pro Bowls with Pittsburgh. He helped win Super Bowl XL and later coached the team’s outside linebackers.

members.name: Maurkice Pouncey
members.text: A 2010 first-round pick who started at center from day one. He made nine Pro Bowls. He anchored the line throughout the 2010s.

members.name: Ben Roethlisberger
members.text: The 11th pick in 2004, he went 13–0 as a rookie starter and won two Super Bowls. His late drive in Super Bowl XLIII ended with the winning touchdown pass to Santonio Holmes. He holds the team’s career passing records.

members.name: Art Rooney Jr.
members.text: The son of the founder, he ran the scouting department from 1965 to 1986. His group built the 1970s dynasty through the draft. That included the 1974 class with four future Hall of Famers.

members.name: Art Rooney Sr.
members.text: Founded the team in 1933 as the Pirates. “The Chief” was known for his loyalty, his cigars and his ties to the city. He saw the team go from decades of struggles to four Super Bowl titles.

members.name: Dan Rooney
members.text: The founder’s son, who ran the team for decades as president and then chairman. He helped hire Chuck Noll and set the team’s steady style. The Rooney Rule for minority hiring is named for him, and he later served as U.S. ambassador to Ireland.

members.name: Andy Russell
members.text: A smart, durable outside linebacker who served in the Army between his rookie season and his return in 1966. He made seven Pro Bowls. He won the first two Super Bowls.

members.name: Donnie Shell
members.text: An undrafted safety from South Carolina State who hit like a linebacker. When he retired, he had more interceptions (51) than any other strong safety in history. He won four Super Bowls and was inducted into Canton in 2020.

members.name: Aaron Smith
members.text: A fourth-round pick who anchored the defensive line at end in the 3-4 for 13 seasons. He did the unglamorous work that let the linebackers rack up sacks. He won two Super Bowls.

members.name: John Stallworth
members.text: A fourth-round pick from Alabama A&M, found through Bill Nunn’s scouting. He caught long touchdowns in Super Bowls XIII and XIV. He was later a part-owner of the team.

members.name: Ernie Stautner
members.text: An undersized but relentless defensive tackle who played 14 seasons in Pittsburgh. He made nine Pro Bowls. He was the face of the franchise in the 1950s.

members.name: Lynn Swann
members.text: A graceful receiver known for acrobatic catches in big games. He was the MVP of Super Bowl X. He won four Super Bowls.

members.name: J.T. Thomas
members.text: A 1973 first-round pick from Florida State who started at cornerback for the 1970s champions. He was a key part of one of the best secondaries in league history. He won four Super Bowl rings.

members.name: Mike Wagner
members.text: An 11th-round pick who became the smart free safety of the Steel Curtain. He led the league with eight interceptions in 1973 and made two Pro Bowls. He won four Super Bowls.

members.name: Hines Ward
members.text: A third-round pick who became the franchise’s all-time leader in catches, receiving yards and receiving touchdowns. He was known for his smile and his punishing blocks. He was the MVP of Super Bowl XL and won two rings.

members.name: Mike Webster
members.text: “Iron Mike” started at center on four Super Bowl champions and made nine Pro Bowls. He set the tone for the offensive line for 15 seasons. He was inducted into Canton in 1997.

members.name: Dwight White
members.text: “Mad Dog” left a hospital bed to play in Super Bowl IX and scored the game’s first points with a safety. He was a fierce defensive end on the Steel Curtain line. He won four Super Bowls.

members.name: Craig Wolfley
members.text: A fifth-round guard from Syracuse who spent the 1980s on the offensive line. He later spent more than two decades on the team’s radio broadcasts, many of them next to his friend Tunch Ilkin. He was inducted into the Hall of Honor in 2026.

members.name: Rod Woodson
members.text: The 10th pick in 1987, he was a shutdown corner and a dangerous returner. He was the 1993 Defensive Player of the Year. He came back from a torn ACL to play in Super Bowl XXX and was inducted into Canton in 2009.
